given.part: An open loan's `dueOn` is before today (UTC)
given.why: Both loans are lent on 2026-03-02, so they are due on 2026-03-16, and the job runs on 2026-03-17, one day after the due date.

given.part: it has no reminder recorded today
given.why: The job runs once on a fresh in-memory database, so neither loan has a reminder recorded before the run.

then.why: If the call were skipped, `fakeNotifications.sent` would be empty and both the arrayContaining and the toHaveLength(2) checks would fail.
Each entry pins `memberId` to the member who borrowed that loan, so sending to any other id fails.

This test can't see the order because the API accepts both calls; recording before asking only shows up on a refusal, and B3's test catches that by checking that the refused loan has no row in reminders.
The reminders table must hold exactly one row for each loan, so dropping the record fails.
`sent_on` is pinned to 2026-03-17, the run date, which differs from the due date of 2026-03-16.

given.part: An open loan already has a reminder recorded today
given.why: The job runs twice on 2026-03-17, so loan1 already has a reminder for today when the second run starts.
loan2 is overdue (due 2026-03-16) and is returned before the run, so being returned is the only thing that excludes it.
The third loan, lent on 2026-03-03, is due on 2026-03-17, the run day itself, which tests the boundary between `<` and `<=`.

then.why: toMatchObject on an array also checks its length, so any extra send (a second one for loan1, or any for loan2 or the third loan) makes it fail.

given.why: The fake refuses loan1 and returns a status-style reason.
The job's test never sets up an unreachable API, but B5 proves that a failed connection comes back as the same `refused` result, and this test covers how the job handles `refused`.

then.why: toEqual pins the whole reminders table to loan2's row alone, so any row for loan1 fails.
toContainEqual requires an entry whose event is exactly `reminder.failed`.
The same entry has its level pinned to `warn`.
`fields` is matched exactly with `loanId: loan1`, so logging a different id fails.
`error` must equal the exact reason the fake gave, so a generic string fails.

then.part: carries on with the other loans
then.why: loan1 is due earlier than loan2 and is the one refused, so stopping after the refusal leaves loan2 unsent and unrecorded, and both checks fail.

given.part: The job has handled every overdue loan
given.why: Three overdue loans, one of them refused, go through a full run before the last log entry is checked.

then.why: The last log entry must have the event `reminders.finished`.
The entry's level is pinned to `info`.
`sent: 2` is asserted, so not counting sends gives 0 and fails.

`fields` is matched with `expect.objectContaining({ sent: 2 })`, so `failed` could be missing, 0 or any other number and the test would still pass, even though the setup refuses one loan; no other test checks this log entry.

given.why: The client is called directly with a complete reminder.

then.why: The recorded method must be `POST`.
The handler only matches `NOTIFICATIONS_PATH` on the NOTIFY_URL host, and the recorded path must be exactly `/notifications`.
The content-type is pinned to `application/json` and the body is parsed as JSON.
The body is compared with toEqual, so renaming or dropping `memberId` fails.
The template value is pinned exactly.
Both `data` keys and their values are matched exactly.
200, 202 and 204 must each come back as `accepted`, so accepting only 200 fails.
A 400 must come back as `refused`, so treating only 5xx as a refusal fails.
A network error must come back as `refused` rather than throwing.

then.part: with a reason naming the status
then.why: The reason must contain `400`, so a generic message fails.

then.part: or saying the API was unreachable
then.why: The reason must contain `unreachable`.
